title: Scheduled and background work
headline: Scheduled work is a fixed floor today, not a load: Supabase calls the app 13,250 times a day and those calls send about 170,000 statements, nearly all finding nothing because the platform is not open, so no feature here should be retired for being unused. The one measured waste is pg_cron's own run log, never pruned: 564 MB, 77% of the 731 MB database, fixed by one small migration (CR-5). What matters at opening is work that grows with stores, pages, products or orders on every run whether or not anything changed: chat knowledge, media, alt texts and product vectors (CR-4), the listings' check that hashes every product on the platform and asks the AI again about unreadable ones every five minutes (CR-15), automations and ad conversions each minute (CR-3), the cookie scan's due check (CR-6), waiting invoices (CR-9) and the accounting loops (CR-16). Calling the six queue routes only when a row waits (CR-1), giving about 30 of the 83 five-minute jobs an hourly or daily cadence with one ledger write a run (CR-2) and holding both with a registry and a scan test (CR-14) keep the floor from growing back; before opening is the cheapest time for all of it.

findings.title: Nine routes are called every minute whether or not anything waits
findings.evidence: pg_cron posts to nine routes every minute: 12,960 calls a day. The ledger says they last took 0 to 72 ms; seven answer before working. Idle paths as read: autopilot 13 statements, broadcasts about 15, integrations about 14, theme-shots 8, cookie-scan 3, dream-factory 2, page-jobs, page-looks and pack-pictures 1 each, plus one ledger upsert per route and one for dream-factory.advance: about 68 a minute. Most queues are also kicked by the request that fills them (site-tools.ts:245, broadcasts/actions.ts:93, support-inbound.ts:148, triggerLook in page-looks.ts:126-139), so the minute poll is mostly a safety net. Six routes have a true queue (a row waits or it does not): page-jobs, page-looks, pack-pictures, dream-factory, theme-shots, cookie-scan. I read each claim statement and wrote its predicate into the fix. The other three (broadcasts, autopilot, integrations) carry several features with time-derived work. Built sizes re-measured in this session from .next: 11 of the 13 scheduled routes require 118 to 145 chunks at start (10.9 to 11.7 MiB of JavaScript); document-pdfs needs 30 chunks (1.5 MiB) and usage 48 (5.0 MiB).
findings.cost: 12,960 invocations a day of functions that are already warm, and about 97,900 idle statements a day. Each call opens fresh connections to the pooler, because idle ones close after 5 s (db/client.ts:14). In database time it is small: net.http_post totals 3,974 s in 78 days, 51 s a day on average and about 150 s a day at today's schedule (estimate). The function size (47 to 125 MiB traced) is paid at deploy and on a cold start, not per call. Estimate: the pool rule keeps an instance running about 5 s per call, about 18 instance-hours a day across the nine routes; what Vercel bills for that was not checked. The floor is flat: it does not grow with stores. Its largest measured consequence is the scheduler's log (CR-5).
findings.who_pays: The server per invocation (Vercel) and the Supabase pooler; the database a little.

findings.title: The dispatcher runs all 83 jobs every five minutes: one cadence for everything, one ledger write per job, five connections
findings.evidence: runJobs() starts 78 jobs at once with Promise.all and five more follow one after another, all with EVERY = 300. Nine are pure prunes with retention of 24 hours to 180 days, though docs/capacity.md:112 puts a prune in the daily cron. About 21 more are tied to a day, an hour or a week (the platform briefing at 07:00 Oslo, staff summaries, analytics alerts, report emails, autopilot reports and budgets, nightly translations, legal upkeep and sources, business changes, recurring invoices, auto-archive, Instagram, platform books, and houseCustomers, which rebuilds the list of every owner and applicant each run). Every job writes its own ledger row: 84 upserts a run, 565,049 so far on a table of about 100 rows. All of it shares a pool of 5 connections: the run takes 1.3 s while the jobs' recorded times sum to 12.1 s, so most recorded time is queueing. A query that waits more than 5 s for a connection throws (pg-pool). Added by the planner: the five trailing jobs and every revalidateTag (route.ts:262-279) wait for the slowest of the 78, and three of those carry budgets of 120 s (sms route.ts:195, legalWrites route.ts:246) and 40 s; so a page scheduled for 09:00 is published in the database at once but its cache is refreshed only when the slowest job ends.
findings.cost: At least 248 statements per idle run (the auditor's floor, not recounted), about 71,400 a day; small in database time. The real exposure is at opening: 83 jobs queue on 5 connections with a 5 s limit, so one job that holds connections for real work can make the others fail with a connection timeout. houseCustomers grows with every owner on the platform, every five minutes.
findings.who_pays: The database and the dispatcher's function, every five minutes; later, the jobs that time out behind a busy one.

findings.title: The cookie scan's due check reads every site every minute without a usable index, and failing sites are retried hourly ahead of healthy ones
findings.evidence: Each minute claimScan() runs two updates and then a statement that lists every open site and, per site, runs two subselects on cookie_scans to find its last scan. Stats: 49,338 calls, 192 s, the fifth most expensive statement; cookie_scans has 1,101,927 sequential scans reading 962 M rows, the most of any table. An index on (store_id, created_at) exists (cookie_scans_store_created_idx), but the subselects compare with 'is not distinct from', which Postgres does not serve from a btree index (confirm with EXPLAIN), so each one reads the table. The schedule started 1,796 scans in 34 to 45 days, 40 to 50 a day, where about ten sites scanned weekly would give under two: a failed scan is retried every hour (RETRY_AFTER) with no back-off, and the pick orders by 'done_at nulls first', so a site that has never scanned well is always taken before a healthy site that is due. The route claims one scan per call.
findings.cost: Today: 3 statements a minute and about 4 s of database time a day; 40 to 50 Chromium runs a day, each up to twelve page renders of our own sites. At opening (estimate from the code): the check is sites times scans-per-site every minute, so a few thousand sites means millions of rows read a minute and then the 15 s statement limit; one scan a minute caps the schedule at 1,440 scans a day, and 60 always-failing sites would take every slot and starve the rest.
findings.who_pays: The database every minute; the server and the storefront functions for each scan.
fix_steps: 1. Check the cause first, read-only: select status, requested_by is null as scheduled, count(*) from commerce.cookie_scans where created_at > now() - interval '7 days' group by 1, 2, and read the failed rows' error. If most scheduled scans are 'failed', the hourly retry is confirmed.

2. Migration and src/db/schema.ts: two indexes on the expression the unique index already uses, coalesce(store_id, the zero uuid): (that, created_at desc), and (that, finished_at desc) where status = 'done'. cookie_scans is not a hot table, so plain create index is allowed.

3. src/server/cookie-scans.ts:86-108: write the two subselects with coalesce(c.store_id, NO_STORE) = coalesce(sites.store_id, NO_STORE) so the indexes serve them. Add 'failures': the site's failed scans since its last done one. Retry after an hour while failures is under 3, then after a day. Order the pick by tried_at nulls first (the site tried longest ago goes first), so a failing site cannot hold the head.

4. Do the weekly pick only in the sweep: claimScan({ pick }) with pick true when the minute is a multiple of 15. In a sweep insert up to 15 due sites as 'queued' in one statement (1,440 a day at most, as today) instead of one as 'running'; the tick's gate (CR-1: a scan is queued) then calls the route each minute until they are done. Move the 'stopped after ten minutes' update into the sweep too. An ordinary minute then costs one statement.
5. src/server/site-cookies.ts:45 (the banner's read of the last done scan, the storefront's query): use the same coalesce form so the new partial index serves it.
6. Reword D58's rule in docs/rules/storefront.md (Cookie consent): weekly, a failed scan tried again after an hour, after a day from the third failure.

findings.title: The listings' check hashes every product on the platform every five minutes, and a listing the AI cannot answer for is asked again every run at the head of the queue
findings.evidence: The dispatcher's contentModeration job ends with screenListings(), Kaizena Flow's own check of listings (DSA art. 7, voluntary), on unless a platform admin turns it off (content_screening defaults to true, line 160). Its candidate statement (lines 205-225) first sorts every row of commerce.product_translations on the platform (distinct on product_id, with title, description and safety text, no store or status filter inside the CTE), then joins every active product of every live store and compares md5(title, description, safety) with the hash kept in content_screened. It is the same 'hash everything to learn nothing changed' shape as the embeddings statement in CR-4, with no store scope, and it runs every five minutes. product_translations has no updated_at, and no trigger moves products.updated_at, so there is no cheaper marker today. For each of up to ten candidates it asks the platform's model once. When the answer is null (a provider error) or cannot be read as the expected JSON (parseScreening returns null, src/lib/content-moderation.ts:103-110), line 230 says 'continue' and nothing is recorded. The candidates are ordered 'screened_at nulls first, p.id', so the same listings come back first on the next run. Triage of notices stops at the first 'no_ai' (line 152); the listings' loop does not stop on a provider error.
findings.cost: Database: one statement every five minutes that reads and sorts every product text on the platform; the like statement for embeddings takes 14.5 ms at today's few hundred translations and cannot use an index for 'hash differs' (estimate: at a few hundred thousand translations it nears the 15 s statement limit, and the job then fails every run). AI: one call per new or changed wording, capped at 10 a run, 2,880 a day, paid on Kaizena Flow's key for every store whatever its plan. The waste: ten listings whose answers cannot be read cost up to 2,880 calls a day for nothing and stop every other listing from being checked; while the provider is down the job makes 10 failing calls a run. How often answers are unreadable in production was not measured.
findings.who_pays: The database every five minutes, in proportion to every store's catalogue; Kaizena Flow's AI bill; and the notices' queue, which silently stops getting flags.
fix_steps: 1. Record a try (smallest, do first). Migration: commerce.content_screened gains tries integer not null default 0 and tried_at timestamptz. In screenListings() (content-moderation.ts:227-231), when the answer is null or unreadable, upsert the row with the hash, flagged false, tries + 1 and tried_at now(), and make the candidate statement leave out a product whose hash is the same and whose tried_at is under a day old. Stop the loop at the first provider error, as triageWaitingReports() does at line 152.

2. Narrow the statement: choose the candidate products first (active products of live stores with no content_screened row, or whose products.text_changed_at is newer than screened_at), limit them, then read the words of those few with a lateral select from product_translations ordered by locale limit 1, and hash only them. products.text_changed_at is the marker of CR-4 step 4 (a trigger on product_translations and product_terms).

3. Until the marker exists: run the listings' check once an hour with a batch of 120 (the same cap of 2,880 a day) through CR-2's cadence. Split runContentModeration() (lines 262-266) so the triage of waiting notices stays at five minutes.
4. Say in docs/dsa.md what the cap means at opening: a move of 5,000 products takes about two days to be read.

src/lib/content-moderation.test.ts (parseScreening) stays. The prompt does not change, so no new agent-eval run or recording is needed (src/server/prompt-versions.ts:102).

findings.title: Six more five-minute jobs re-check every store that has the feature on, and the ledger's order never rotates
findings.evidence: The verified report's clean list says only the loops of CR-3, CR-4, CR-6 and CR-9 grow. A scan of all 83 job functions for loops (scratch script, then each read) finds six more that do per-store work on every run. ledger: for every book that is open or closed in the last 60 days, one statement with ten 'union all' branches over invoices, credit notes, payments, refunds, payouts and disputes with two anti-joins (ledger.ts:555-611), then a read of the store's Tripletex connection (ledger-compare.ts:51); the books are taken 'order by updated_at' inside a 40 s budget, and the job never moves updated_at (only the owner's own edits do: ledger.ts:191 and 428, vat-return.ts:138), so the order is the same on every run. tripletex and fiken: for every connected store, the connection, two or more 'sweep' inserts, a claim and an 'attention' count, at least five statements, one store after another in 40 s (ordered by last_ok_at, which is fair). autoArchive: for every store with the option on, a candidates query over orders with four correlated subqueries, though its cutoff is whole days. autopilotBudgets: for every store with an AI budget, a sum over the month's ai_usage, for an email sent at most twice a month. recurring: for every store with an active repeating invoice, two reads, though periods are days. What is done well in the same files: a document that cannot be posted waits a day before the next try (ledger.ts:606-607), and Tripletex opens no session when a store has nothing to send.
findings.cost: Nothing for a store that does not use these features: the cost follows use, which is the right shape. For stores that do, it is paid per run and not per change. Estimate from the code: 1,000 stores with books and Tripletex are about 7,000 statements every five minutes, one after another inside 40 s budgets. Once the first books in the fixed order have real work that fills the 40 s, the books after them are not reached, run after run.
findings.who_pays: The database every five minutes, in proportion to the stores that use books, Tripletex, Fiken, auto-archive, an AI budget or repeating invoices; later, the owner whose book is last in the order.
fix_steps: 1. Ledger order (smallest, do first). Migration: commerce.ledger_books gains checked_at timestamptz. runLedgerPosting() (ledger.ts:1042-1046) orders by checked_at nulls first and sets checked_at = now() for each book after its turn, so every book gets a turn before any gets a second.

2. Skip an idle book cheaply: in the same first statement keep only books whose store has a document, payment, refund or payout newer than checked_at (five 'exists' on created_at or issued_at), or whose ledger_waiting rows are due their daily retry, or that were last checked over an hour ago. An idle book then costs nothing between hourly looks.

3. tripletex and fiken (tripletex-sync.ts:649-655, fiken-sync.ts:524-530): the same narrowing in the list statement: a store with an invoice or credit note issued since last_ok_at, a sync row not yet 'synced', or last looked at over an hour ago. Read docs/tripletex.md and docs/fiken.md first for any promised delay (the '40 seconds' in the dispatcher's comment is the run's budget, not a promise).
4. autoArchive, autopilotBudgets and recurring: hourly cadence in CR-2's list (their units are days and months).

findings.title: The daily job runs about 40 functions in one request under one ledger row, so a prune that fails is not seen
findings.evidence: Counted in the route: 13 functions start at once (line 61), 8 run one after another (lines 63-78), then 19 start at once (line 79): 40 in all, of which 24 are prunes. Two ledger rows cover them: route.subscription-reminders and daily.database-door. docs/capacity.md:112 asks that a prune 'never throws', and most obey by catching their own error: pruneVisits() logs a warning and returns what it managed (analytics-visits.ts:339-341); runRetention() keeps a failed step in its answer and the audit log (retention.ts:540-543); 19 calls in the route catch with console.error and answer 0 or an empty result (lines 69-79). So a prune that fails every day leaves a log line, and the ledger says the day went well. The first group has no catch at all: pruneUsage() is one unbatched delete with no try (ai-usage.ts:107-110), and if it or any of the other twelve throws, the request answers 500 and the retention schedule, the erasure resumes, the privacy reminders and the 19 prunes after it do not run that day. Both groups share five connections with a 5 s wait limit (db/client.ts:68-70), as in CR-2. pruneVisits() also loops over every store, closed ones included, with two deletes each, one after another.
findings.cost: No running cost today: it runs once a day. The exposure is the review's own subject: retention is the only brake on table growth (24 prunes) and part of the GDPR schedule (D162), and nothing shows per job whether it ran, failed or removed anything. cron.job_run_details (CR-5) is what a table looks like when nobody sees a missing prune.
findings.who_pays: The database later, in tables that grow unseen; the platform's admins, who hear of a failed day but not which job; owners and shoppers if an erasure or a retention step is skipped.
